REP: Grace, good to see you. Before anything else, how did the BP-200 check day go last month?
CUSTOMER: Better than I expected. We checked about forty people and sold eleven monitors that week. A couple of them were brand-new hypertension patients we'd never have caught otherwise. One of them came back last week just to thank us, because her doctor changed her medication after seeing the log.
REP: That's great to hear. What did you learn from the people who came in?
CUSTOMER: That people want us to do more of that kind of thing. Three different people asked if we do flu tests. One woman was annoyed that we didn't, actually. She said the urgent care quoted her a three-hour wait, so she just went home without a test.
REP: How did your team handle those requests?
CUSTOMER: We apologized and sent them to urgent care. My staff hated it. They felt like we were turning people away. My senior tech actually asked me afterwards why we don't do testing, since we do everything else.
REP: That's the reason I wanted to show you RapidPanel. It's the same idea as the check day, but for strep, flu and COVID, on one reader, with results in about ten minutes. You'd charge thirty-five to forty dollars cash and the kits cost about twelve.
CUSTOMER: I'd like to offer it, but I only have one consultation room and the vaccine clinic uses it three afternoons a week. On the other days I use it for medication reviews, so it's booked more than people realize.
REP: Understood. The test itself doesn't need the room for long. The swab takes two minutes and the reader can sit at the counter while it runs, so most stores swab in the consultation room and run the reader behind the counter. That way the room is only tied up for a couple of minutes per patient.
CUSTOMER: Two minutes I can find. Even on vaccine days. And the reader behind the counter is fine, we have room next to the fax machine.
REP: What's your biggest concern about getting started?
CUSTOMER: Training. I have two new techs and I don't want to throw too much at them before flu season. They're still learning the register and the insurance rejections. If I pile something else on now, I'm worried one of them quits.
REP: That makes sense, especially with new people. Which of your team would you want trained first?
CUSTOMER: My senior tech, Luis, and myself. The new techs can shadow later. Luis has been here eight years and he's great with anxious parents.
REP: Then we'd start with just you and Luis. The online module is forty-five minutes, and our clinical trainer does a one-hour session here in the store. The new techs can do the online module whenever they're ready. Would that pace work for your team?
CUSTOMER: That pace works. Luis would actually love it.
REP: Great. Let's get the CLIA paperwork moving now, since that's the long pole. It usually takes three to six weeks. I'll bring the pre-filled packet on Friday the 9th at eleven, we can sign it together, and I'll book the in-store training for the week after it's approved. Does Friday at eleven work?
CUSTOMER: Friday at eleven is fine. Luis is on that day.
REP: Perfect. I'll email you the training outline tonight so Luis can see what he's signing up for.
CUSTOMER: Thanks, Maya. Good timing on this.
